Every connected graph on $n$ vertices can be partitioned into at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ edge-disjoint paths.
#583: [Er71,p.101]
graph theory
A problem of Erdős and Gallai. If we drop the edge-disjoint condition then this conjecture was proved by Fan [Fa02].
There are many partial results towards this conjecture. We list some highlights below; $G$ is an arbitrary connected graph on $n$ vertices.
 Lovász [Lo68] proved that $G$ can be partitioned into at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ edge-disjoint paths and cycles, and hence into at most $n-1$ paths. This also implies the original conjecture if $G$ has at most one vertex of even degree. 
 Chung [Ch78] proved that $G$ can be partitioned into at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ edge-disjoint trees.
 Pyber [Py96] proved that $G$ can be covered by at most $n/2+O(n^{3/4})$ paths (that may not be edge-disjoint).
 Pyber [Py96] also proved the original conjecture if the subgraph induced by vertices of even degree is a forest.
 Bonamy and Perrett [BoPe19] proved the conjecture if $G$ has maximum degree $\leq 5$.
 Blanché, Bonamy, and Bonichon [BBB21] proved this conjecture if $G$ is planar.
 Anto and Basavaraju [AnBa23] proved the conjecture if $G$ is $2$-degenerate (every subgraph has a vertex of degree $\leq 2$).
 Chu, Fan, and Zhou [CFZ26] proved the conjecture if the subgraph induced by vertices of even degree is $K_m$ for some $m\leq 15$ and $n$ is odd.
 Dean and Kouider [DeKo00] prove that $\lceil \frac{2}{3}n\rceil$ edge-disjoint paths always suffice, even for disconnected graphs (for which this bound is optimal). The same bound was independently obtained by Yan in their 1998 PhD thesis.
Hajós [Lo68] has conjectured that if $G$ has all degrees even then $G$ can be partitioned into at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ edge-disjoint cycles.
See also [184] for an analogous problem decomposing into edges and cycles and [1017] for decomposing into complete graphs. See also the entry in the graphs problem collection.

 An exhaustive check at small $n$, and the reason it is not vacuous.
The conjecture holds for every connected graph on at most $11$ vertices: $11{,}716{,}571$ graphs at $n = 10$ and $1{,}006{,}700{,}565$ at $n = 11$, no counterexample and nothing left undecided. Each sweep is split into seven shards, and the run is only accepted if the shard counts sum to the number of connected graphs, OEIS A001349; that equality is the exhaustiveness certificate and a mismatch aborts the run.
The obvious objection is that the partial results already listed on this page might cover everything that small. For $n \le 6$ they do, so a check there establishes nothing. But applying all six to every connected graph gives:
$n = 7$: $36$ of $853$ settled by none of them. $n = 8$: $2{,}058$ of $11{,}117$. $n = 9$: $89{,}757$ of $261{,}080$. $n = 10$: $6{,}666{,}730$ of $11{,}716{,}571$, a majority.
So from $n = 7$ upward the check covers graphs that Lovász, Pyber, Bonamy-Perrett, Blanché-Bonamy-Bonichon, Anto-Basavaraju and Chu-Fan-Zhou between them do not reach, and the uncovered fraction grows with $n$. I could not find a published exhaustive verification for small $n$, though that is a negative search rather than a proof that none exists.
Two things I would want checked before anyone relies on this. The decision is over simple paths, not trails; the trail version follows from an Euler argument and is much easier, so a decider that quietly allowed repeated vertices would report success on everything. An independent decider written from the definition re-decides all $992$ connected graphs on $4$ to $7$ vertices and agrees with the fast one throughout. Beyond $n = 7$ that cross-check has not been run, and the result rests on the C decider together with the A001349 count.
$n = 12$ is not settled. The sweep itself is complete and exhaustive, $164{,}059{,}830{,}476$ graphs, but it leaves $35{,}633{,}639$ that the heuristic cannot decide, and on a random sample of those the exhaustive decider averages $2.61$ seconds each, about $154$ days on seven cores. Worse, $3.25\%$ of the sample exceeded the decider's node cap, so roughly a million graphs would have come back undecided and no verification would have followed even after the wait.
Code, run records and a standalone audit (REPRODUCE.md):
https://github.com/sallerk/erdos-notes/tree/main/p583
Disclosure: the searches and computations were done with AI assistance.

 As far as I can tell, the best result without any further restrictions on $G$ comes from this paper by Dean and Kouider, where they show that $\left \lfloor \frac{2}{3}n \right \rfloor$ edge-disjoint paths suffice. I found various sources claiming that Yan obtained the same upper bound of $\left \lfloor \frac{2}{3}n \right \rfloor$ in their PhD thesis titled On path decompositions of graphs, but I couldn't find it online. 
This result even holds for disconnected graphs by the way, in which case it is actually optimal.

 L. Pyber in [Py85] has proved this conjecture for graphs whose even-degree vertices induce a forest.
X. Geng, M. Fang and D. Li in [GFL15] have proved this conjecture for a maximal outerplanar graph or a 2-connected outerplanar graph.
M. Bonamy and T. J. Perrett in [BoPe19] have proved this conjecture for graphs with maximum degree at most 5.
A. Blanche, M. Bonamy and N. Bonichon in [BBB21] have proved this conjecture for planar graphs.
Y. Chu, G. Fan and Q. Liu in [CFL21] have proved this conjecture for graphs with maximum degree at most 6 in which the vertices of maximum degree form an independent set (with some exceptions).
